name: Plasticine
basis: why: a modeller builds a scene from separate pieces pressed side by side; how: k-means clay colours, each region puffed, thumb dents

lumenary.blurb: Pieces of modelling clay pressed side by side: flat colours, puffed up and glossy, with thumb dents.

facts.bestOn: Bold subjects with a few distinct colour regions

why: Modelling clay comes in a handful of flat colours, so the picture is first reduced to a small box of them. Each region of one colour is then puffed up into its own pillow, dented with thumbs and lit, which is how a modeller builds a scene out of separate pieces pressed side by side.
how: Blur lightly and find the k most typical colours with k-means, made more saturated and pulled towards the middle of lightness.
Give each pixel its nearest colour and remove isolated specks by a majority vote of neighbours.
Treat each region as a mask, blur it twice so it is high in the middle and low at the rim, and raise it to the power 1.5 for a rounded top.
Subtract soft round hollows at random places and add a little low-frequency noise for hand-worked unevenness.
Light the height map with one diffuse light and a tight highlight, and darken creases where neighbouring pieces differ.
history: Plasticine was invented by William Harbutt in Bath, England, in 1897 and sold as a non-drying modelling material for schools. It later became the favourite of stop-motion animators, notably at Aardman Animations, whose character Morph appeared on British television in the 1970s and whose Wallace and Gromit films followed in 1989.
terms: A method that finds a few representative colours by repeatedly averaging groups of pixels.
A small, bright reflection of a light on a glossy surface.
Animation made by photographing a model one small move at a time.
paragraphs: Modelling clay comes in a few flat colours, so the picture is first reduced to a small box of them. The pixels are blurred a little, k-means finds the k most typical colours (made more saturated and pulled toward the middle of the lightness range, like fresh clay), every pixel takes its nearest colour, and a majority vote over neighbouring pixels removes isolated specks. What is left is a map of regions, each one piece of clay.

Each region is then puffed up into its own pillow. The region’s mask (1 inside, 0 outside) is blurred twice, so it is high in the middle and falls away at the rim, and raised to the power 1.5 to round the top. Soft round hollows (thumb dents) are subtracted at random places and a little low-frequency noise adds the hand-worked unevenness. The slope of that height map gives a surface normal, which is lit with one diffuse light and a tight specular highlight (the gloss slider). Pixels whose neighbours two steps away belong to a different piece are darkened, which draws the creases between pieces.

equations.tex: h(\mathbf x)=\Big(\operatorname{blur}^{2}(m_c)\Big)^{1.5}(\mathbf x)\ \ \text{inside piece } c,\qquad h\leftarrow h-a\,e^{-\lVert\mathbf x-\mathbf c\rVert^{2}/r^{2}}
equations.note: The pillow height of piece c from its mask m_c, and a thumb dent of depth a and radius r at c.
Shading: κ is 0.72 on a seam and 1 elsewhere.
Gloss highlight; g is the gloss slider and m the half vector between light and viewer.

presets.text: Fewer colours of clay give a chunkier, more toy-like picture.
High gloss and deep dents make it look freshly handled.
Move the light to the top and see the pillows change.
